summary:
The Faroe Islands is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Danish national criminal law and document rules apply here; equality and family law are set locally by the Løgting.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1933, when it was decriminalised across the Kingdom of Denmark. The age of consent for male same-sex relations was then fixed at 18. The Faroe Islands did not follow Denmark's 1977 move to a gender-neutral age of 15 until 1988, and the age of consent has stood at a gender-neutral 15 ever since.

Since 1 January 2007 anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation is liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. On the sourced account this made the Faroe Islands the last Northern European country to adopt such a protection. Gender identity does not appear among the grounds the provision lists.

Two incidents of anti-LGBT violence are documented. In 2006 the openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out; he and his family then received threatening telephone calls, and police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, became mentally ill and died by suicide in 2012. In 2005 the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically assaulting them in Tórshavn, and nowhere else had the group been attacked. The most recent incident documented in these sources dates from 2006; no later instance is documented.

Hostility voiced by public figures is on the record. In June 2015 Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni published a letter to the editor, 'Hvar eru vit á veg?', attacking the public broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as 'non-culture' while asking whether 'these people do not feel any shame'. Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana has repeatedly compared LGBT Føroyar to the Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters, urged that the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the centre, and in 2015 demanded that Pride be banned; the singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him.
tangentialFactors:
Activism has run at a scale unusual for a territory of roughly 47,000 people. In November 2006 PinkNews reported that LGBT activists had gathered around 20,000 online signatures demanding an end to sexual-orientation discrimination and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics; at that date the Faroe Islands had neither, leaving homophobia legally unaddressed.

After the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen an internet petition collected 20,000 signatures, and eight women in Tórshavn gathered a further 2,000 by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations. A petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures. These are raw counts against a small population, so they indicate the volume of signatures rather than a per-capita measure of opinion.

Religiously motivated opposition has surfaced at the level of state ceremony. In September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for the visiting Icelandic prime minister Johanna Sigurdardóttir and her partner, citing his religion. The first gay pride march, held in 2005, provoked substantial controversy.
localsOnly:
The provision in force since 1 January 2007 binds the speech of residents as well as visitors: a public statement that threatens, insults or degrades a group on grounds including sexual orientation carries a fine or up to two years' imprisonment.

Equality and family law are made by the Løgting rather than in Copenhagen, so the rules on partnership and marriage for residents are set locally. The inventory does not state what those rules currently are.

The refusal of police to handle the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen followed from the absence of any local anti-discrimination law at the time; that gap has been filled since 1 January 2007, and no later account of police declining a case appears in these sources.

Local protection is framed on sexual orientation. Gender identity and gender expression are not named among the protected grounds in the sourced text, so a trans resident seeking redress under this provision would not be covered on its face.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Faroe Islands now recognises registered partnerships or same-sex marriage is unresolved here. The sources document only the absence of such a law in 2006 and a petition against same-sex marriage of 1,262 signatures, which the source does not date.

Whether gender identity or gender expression is a protected ground under any Faroese provision, and whether local hate-crime law covers anti-trans conduct, is not sourced.

The inventory contains nothing on entry or visa requirements, passport or ID marker rules, airport screening, healthcare access, or facilities for trans visitors to the Faroe Islands. Danish document rules are stated to apply, but no detail on marker-change requirements appears in these sources.

No data is available on enforcement, charges or sentencing under the 1 January 2007 provision, and no trans-specific violence statistics for the Faroe Islands appear in the inventory. The violence evidence consists of individual incidents in 2005 and 2006.
